notes.meaning: After King Nebuchadnezzar deported King Jeconiah, the royal court, and the skilled metalworkers to Babylon in 597 BC, God gave Jeremiah a vision. The prophet saw two baskets of figs set right before the Lord's temple in Jerusalem. Placing them at the temple recalled the baskets used for firstfruit offerings, bringing the whole nation before God for His evaluation.

One basket held choice, early-ripening figs, while the other basket was filled with rotten figs that could not be eaten. Early figs were prized as a rare and sweet delicacy in Judah, gathered weeks before the regular summer harvest. By setting the finest fruit next to spoiled fruit, God showed that the people were heading toward two completely opposite outcomes.

The Lord asked Jeremiah what he saw, and the prophet replied that the good figs were very good, and the bad figs were completely inedible. God directed Jeremiah's attention to the sharp contrast between the two baskets before explaining them. This made it clear that God was dividing the nation into two distinct groups, with no middle ground between them.

The word of the Lord came directly to Jeremiah to explain the vision. Jeremiah did not have to guess what the two baskets represented or rely on his own human intuition. God spoke His own explanation so the prophet could understand what lay ahead for Judah.

The Lord revealed that the good figs represented the captives already deported to Babylon. The people remaining in Jerusalem assumed that the exiles were cursed and that they themselves were God's favored remnant. God turned that human thinking upside down, announcing that He sent those captives to Babylon for their own preservation and good.

God promised to keep His watchful eye on the captives in Babylon, bring them back to Judah, and plant them securely. Instead of abandoning them, God intended to protect them in exile and eventually bring their children home. This began to take place when the exiles returned after seventy years to rebuild their community.

God promised to give the exiles an inward heart to know Him, restoring them to a devoted covenant relationship where they would belong to Him completely. Through the discipline of exile, God would cure them of idolatry and lead them to sincere repentance. True spiritual renewal always begins inside the heart through God's gracious work.

differ.view: Reformed Christians understand this verse as evidence that true repentance and a changed heart are entirely God's sovereign gift, since fallen human beings cannot turn to God through their own free will.

notes.meaning: The Lord declared that the bad, rotten figs represented King Zedekiah, his leaders, and the people still living in Jerusalem or hiding in Egypt. Zedekiah and his court refused to listen to Jeremiah's warnings, choosing instead to trust in political alliances with Egypt. Because of their stubborn rebellion against God's word, they were marked for complete ruin.

God warned that He would make these rebellious survivors an object of dread, shame, and mockery among all surrounding kingdoms. Rather than finding safety in Jerusalem or Egypt, they would suffer the public humiliation described in the ancient covenant curses of Moses. Their downfall would stand as a warning to the nations of what happens when people stubbornly reject God.

The Lord declared that He would send war, starvation, and deadly sickness against those who stayed behind until they vanished from the land. These three classic judgments would remove the rebellious remnant from the very inheritance God had given to their ancestors. This warning was fulfilled in 586 BC when the Babylonian army destroyed Jerusalem and burned its temple.
